# Lab 8 — Chaos Engineering: Break Things on Purpose

## Setup — Mixed Load Baseline

The Lab 8 mixed load generator was applied to exercise the full QuickTicket flow: event listing, reservation, and payment.

```text
deployment.apps/mixedload unchanged
deployment "mixedload" successfully rolled out
mixedload   2/2   2 available
mixedload-96c9f49fd-hqnp9   1/1   Running
mixedload-96c9f49fd-mvczq   1/1   Running
```

Baseline Prometheus query from inside the cluster:

```text
kubectl exec -n monitoring deployment/prometheus -- wget -qO- 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(gateway_requests_total[1m]))'
```

Observed baseline:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{},"value":[1791121118.938,"10.220588309332305"]}]}}
```

The baseline gateway request rate was approximately 10.22 RPS before starting the chaos experiments.

<img alt="Task 1 setup baseline RPS" src="data:image/png;base64," />

## Task 1 — Three Chaos Experiments

### Experiment 1 — Pod Kill Under Load

#### Hypothesis

If I delete one gateway pod while traffic is flowing, Kubernetes will create a replacement pod and the Service will keep routing traffic to the remaining gateway pods. I expect little or no 5xx impact because the gateway has 5 replicas and only one pod is removed.

#### Method

```text
VICTIM=$(kubectl get pods -l app=gateway -o name | head -1)
echo "Killing $VICTIM at $(date +%H:%M:%S)"
kubectl delete "$VICTIM"
```

Observed output:

```text
Killing pod/gateway-6d69f5f9fb-dw28n at 13:40:23
pod "gateway-6d69f5f9fb-dw28n" deleted from default namespace
```

#### Observations

A replacement gateway pod became Ready in less than 10 seconds after the victim pod was deleted.

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 1 pod kill recovery" src="data:image/png;base64," />

Prometheus query for gateway 5xx responses:

```text
kubectl exec -n monitoring deployment/prometheus -- wget -qO- 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum(increase(gateway_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[3m]))'
```

Observed output:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{},"value":[1791121999.073,"9.257801192568268"]}]}}
```

Prometheus reported approximately 9 gateway 5xx responses in the 3-minute window after the pod kill. The value is fractional because Prometheus extrapolates `increase()` over the selected time window.

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 1 5xx after pod kill" src="data:image/png;base64," />

Prometheus query for per-pod traffic:

```text
kubectl exec -n monitoring deployment/prometheus -- wget -qO- 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum%20by%20%28pod%29%20%28rate%28gateway_requests_total%5B1m%5D%29%29'
```

Observed output:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{"pod":"gateway-6d69f5f9fb-zqqp4"},"value":[1791122228.651,"1.9182048498009412"]},{"metric":{"pod":"gateway-6d69f5f9fb-rxh2h"},"value":[1791122228.651,"1.5761852734144113"]},{"metric":{"pod":"gateway-6d69f5f9fb-hnghx"},"value":[1791122228.651,"1.9182395627861524"]},{"metric":{"pod":"gateway-6d69f5f9fb-jqhmg"},"value":[1791122228.651,"1.5380161401223176"]},{"metric":{"pod":"gateway-6d69f5f9fb-24zkq"},"value":[1791122228.651,"2.008686210640608"]}]}}
```

Traffic was distributed across 5 gateway pods after recovery. The replacement pod `gateway-6d69f5f9fb-24zkq` was already receiving traffic, which confirms that the Service added it back to the endpoint set after it became Ready.

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 1 per-pod traffic after pod kill" src="data:image/png;base64," />

#### Comparison and resilience improvement

The hypothesis was mostly correct. Kubernetes recreated a replacement pod quickly, and the Service distributed traffic across all available gateway pods after recovery. The surprising part was that the transition was not completely error-free: Prometheus reported approximately 9 gateway 5xx responses in the 3-minute window after the pod deletion.

To improve resilience against this failure, I would investigate why some requests returned 5xx during pod replacement and tune gateway termination/readiness behavior, such as graceful shutdown and readiness removal before termination, so in-flight requests are less likely to fail.

### Experiment 2 — Payment Latency Injection

#### Hypothesis

If payments takes 2 seconds per request, checkout payments will become slower but should not return 5xx, because the injected latency of 2000ms is still below the gateway timeout of 5000ms. I expect the p99 latency for `/pay` to increase, while `/events` should remain mostly unaffected.

#### Method

```text
kubectl set env deployment/payments PAYMENT_LATENCY_MS=2000
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments --timeout=30s
```

Observed output:

```text
deployment.apps/payments env updated
Waiting for deployment "payments" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
Waiting for deployment "payments" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "payments" successfully rolled out
```

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 2 payment latency injected" src="data:image/png;base64," />

#### Observations

Prometheus query for gateway error rate:

```text
kubectl exec -n monitoring deployment/prometheus -- wget -qO- 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(gateway_requests_total%7Bstatus%3D~%225..%22%7D%5B1m%5D))/sum(rate(gateway_requests_total%5B1m%5D))'
```

Observed output:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{},"value":[1791122671.973,"0.002000026042747031"]}]}}
```

The gateway error-rate ratio was approximately 0.002, or 0.2%, during the 2-second payments latency injection.

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 2 payment latency error rate" src="data:image/png;base64," />

Prometheus query for p99 latency by path:

```text
kubectl exec -n monitoring deployment/prometheus -- wget -qO- 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.99,+sum+by+(le,path)+(rate(gateway_request_duration_seconds_bucket%5B1m%5D)))'
```

Observed output:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{"path":"/events"},"value":[1791122801.576,"0.6391887701781708"]},{"metric":{"path":"/events/{id}/reserve"},"value":[1791122801.576,"3.3117659245856794"]},{"metric":{"path":"/reserve/{id}/pay"},"value":[1791122801.576,"NaN"]},{"metric":{"path":"/health"},"value":[1791122801.576,"2.2250016985958982"]}]}}
```

The highest measured p99 latency was on `/events/{id}/reserve`, at approximately 3.31 seconds. `/events` stayed lower, at approximately 0.64 seconds. `/reserve/{id}/pay` returned `NaN`, which means there were not enough successful payment-path samples in that 1-minute histogram window to compute a p99 value.

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 2 p99 latency by path" src="data:image/png;base64," />

The bonus timeout observation was also attempted by setting `PAYMENT_LATENCY_MS=6000`:

```text
kubectl set env deployment/payments PAYMENT_LATENCY_MS=6000
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments --timeout=30s
```

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 2 payment latency beyond timeout injected" src="data:image/png;base64," />

The aggregate error rate remained low:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{},"value":[1791123015.888,"0.0020280682596347317"]}]}}
```

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 2 payment latency beyond timeout error rate" src="data:image/png;base64," />

A more specific query by path and status showed why the timeout was not visible as 504s in that window:

```json
{"status":"success","data":{"resultType":"vector","result":[{"metric":{"path":"/health","status":"200"},"value":[1791123092.738,"0.9415002627946786"]},{"metric":{"path":"/events","status":"200"},"value":[1791123092.738,"4.019472713160285"]},{"metric":{"path":"/health","status":"503"},"value":[1791123092.738,"0.054313716027709374"]},{"metric":{"path":"/events/{id}/reserve","status":"200"},"value":[1791123092.738,"0"]},{"metric":{"path":"/reserve/{id}/pay","status":"200"},"value":[1791123092.738,"0"]},{"metric":{"path":"/events/{id}/reserve","status":"409"},"value":[1791123092.738,"4.001380707107305"]},{"metric":{"path":"/events","status":"502"},"value":[1791123092.738,"0"]}]}}
```

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 2 payment latency beyond timeout by path and status" src="data:image/png;base64," />

During the 6000ms observation window, the load mostly hit `/events` and `/events/{id}/reserve`; reservations returned `409`, so the flow did not reach `/reserve/{id}/pay` often enough to observe 504s. This showed that the payment timeout was hidden by an earlier bottleneck in the checkout path.

#### Comparison and resilience improvement

The main 2000ms latency hypothesis was mostly correct: the aggregate gateway error rate stayed low because the payment latency was still below the gateway timeout. The latency observations showed partial degradation instead of a broad outage. The result also exposed a measurement limitation: the payment path did not have enough samples in the observed window, and later the 6000ms timeout scenario was masked by reservation conflicts.

To improve resilience against this failure, I would add a latency-based SLO and alert for checkout paths, especially p95/p99 latency on `/reserve/{id}/pay` and `/events/{id}/reserve`, because slow successful requests can hurt users before error-rate alerts fire.

### Experiment 3 — Redis Failure

#### Hypothesis

If Redis goes down, users should still be able to list events because reads come from PostgreSQL, but reservations should fail because Redis is required to hold temporary ticket reservations. The health endpoint should report degraded dependency status.

#### Method

```text
kubectl scale deployment/redis --replicas=0
kubectl get pods -l app=redis -w
```

Observed output:

```text
deployment.apps/redis scaled
redis-6fcfb5475d-dj8hs   1/1   Terminating
redis-6fcfb5475d-dj8hs   0/1   Completed
```

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 3 Redis scaled down" src="data:image/png;base64," />

#### Observations

The probe from inside the cluster could not connect to the `gateway` Service:

```text
GET /events:
curl: (7) Failed to connect to gateway:8080 after 2055 ms: Could not connect to server
POST /reserve:
curl: (7) Failed to connect to gateway:8080 after 1012 ms: Could not connect to server
GET /health:
curl: (7) Failed to connect to gateway:8080 after 1015 ms: Could not connect to server
command terminated with exit code 7
```

<img alt="Task 1 experiment 3 Redis failure probe" src="data:image/png;base64," />

Follow-up Kubernetes inspection showed the reason:

```text
gateway pods: 0/1 Running
gateway endpoints: empty
Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
```

All gateway pods were still running, but they were not Ready because the readiness probe calls `/health`, and `/health` returned 503 while Redis was unavailable. Since no gateway pods were Ready, the `gateway` Service had no endpoints, so even read-only `/events` traffic through the gateway could not be served.

After Redis was restored, the gateway recovered:

```text
gateway-6d69f5f9fb-24zkq   1/1   Running
gateway-6d69f5f9fb-hnghx   1/1   Running
gateway-6d69f5f9fb-jqhmg   1/1   Running
gateway-6d69f5f9fb-rxh2h   1/1   Running
gateway-6d69f5f9fb-zqqp4   1/1   Running
gateway endpoints: 10.42.0.54:8080,10.42.0.56:8080,10.42.0.57:8080 + 2 more
```

#### Comparison and resilience improvement

The hypothesis was only partially correct. Redis failure did break reservations as expected, but the bigger surprise was that listing events through the gateway also became unavailable. The reason was not that `/events` directly needs Redis; it was that the gateway readiness probe depends on `/health`, and `/health` became 503 when a downstream dependency was unhealthy. Kubernetes then removed all gateway pods from the Service endpoint set.

To improve resilience against this failure, I would decouple readiness from non-critical downstream dependency health. The gateway should stay Ready when it can still serve read-only traffic, while `/health` or a separate dependency-health endpoint can report Redis degradation for alerts and dashboards.


## Task 2 — Combined Failure Scenario

### Scenario design

I tested the lab's degraded dependencies scenario because it combines failures on two different parts of the request path while the system is under additional load. The scenario injected a 30% payment failure rate and 500 ms payment latency, capped the `events` service database connections at 3, and scaled `mixedload` to 3 replicas.

The goal was to see how the system behaves when a dependency is unreliable, another service has reduced database capacity, and traffic is higher than the baseline. This is closer to a real incident than a single isolated failure, because production outages often happen when multiple small degradations stack together.

My hypothesis was that latency would react first, especially on `/events/{id}/reserve`, because reservation requests are more dependent on shared backend capacity than simple event listing. I expected the error rate to increase as well, but not necessarily dominate the incident unless the payment failures or database connection cap caused sustained 5xx responses.

### Failure injection

```bash
kubectl set env deployment/payments PAYMENT_FAILURE_RATE=0.3 PAYMENT_LATENCY_MS=500
kubectl set env deployment/events DB_MAX_CONNS=3
kubectl scale deployment/mixedload --replicas=3
kubectl rollout status deployment/payments --timeout=30s
kubectl rollout status deployment/events --timeout=30s
```

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Task 2 combined failure injection and rollout status" />

The rollout completed successfully for both `payments` and `events`, so the measurements were taken after the degraded configuration was active.

### Observations over the 3-5 minute window

I sampled the Prometheus error-rate and p99-latency queries repeatedly during the observation window.

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Task 2 repeated Prometheus samples for error rate and p99 latency" />

The first complete sample was taken at `2026-10-04 14:52:05 UTC`. The gateway 5xx ratio was `0.008646327957319358`, which is approximately 0.86%. The p99 latency values were:

```text
/health                 0.6812497533455352 s
/events                 0.2975034535543807 s
/events/{id}/reserve   0.539995436195346 s
/reserve/{id}/pay      NaN
```

A later sample around `2026-10-04 14:53:22 UTC` kept the error rate at about the same level: `0.00878243851650464`, or approximately 0.88%.

The final complete sample was taken at `2026-10-04 14:54:04 UTC`. The gateway 5xx ratio was `0.0070523016881477215`, or approximately 0.71%. The p99 latency values were:

```text
/health                 0.4724992000901705 s
/events                 0.23607958814013458 s
/events/{id}/reserve   0.7150080217602458 s
/reserve/{id}/pay      NaN
```

The first golden signal that clearly reacted was latency. The error rate did increase, but it stayed below 1% in the observed samples. Latency showed clearer route-level impact, especially on `/events/{id}/reserve`.

### Worst latency amplification

The worst useful p99 latency was on `/events/{id}/reserve`, which reached about 0.715 seconds in the final sample. `/events` stayed lower, around 0.236 to 0.298 seconds in the complete samples. `/reserve/{id}/pay` returned `NaN`, so I cannot honestly claim it was better or worse from this evidence; there were not enough payment samples in the measured window for Prometheus to calculate a valid p99 for that path.

### Weakest link and resilience improvement

The weakest link in this combined scenario was the reservation path handled by the `events` service. The evidence points to `/events/{id}/reserve` as the path with the strongest latency amplification when database capacity was capped and traffic was increased. The payment degradation contributed to overall risk, but the measured `/pay` series did not have enough valid samples to identify it as the weakest path from this run.

To make this scenario more resilient, I would first protect the reservation path with stricter timeout and backpressure behavior. The `events` service should fail fast when its database pool is saturated instead of allowing requests to queue long enough to amplify tail latency. I would also expose database pool saturation metrics directly, so alerts can distinguish between a payment dependency problem and an `events` database-capacity problem.
